sections.heading: What this SQL query generator does
sections.body:
This page turns a request in plain English into a SQL query. You say what you need, such as a list of orders from last month or the total sales for each region. The generator writes the query for the database you name, so the SQL uses that database's syntax.

You can add table names and columns if you know them. Without them, the generator has to guess your names, so type them in when you can. The answer usually comes back in about 1 to 3 seconds, and the SQL can be copied with one click.

The tool is built for writing queries. It does not replace checking them. Read the SQL, compare it with your real table and column names, and test it on a copy of your data before you use it on a live database.

sections.heading: How to generate a query
sections.body:
Open the [SQL query generator](https://sql-generator.lazur.app/) and follow these steps.

1. Type what you need in the box labeled What do you need?
2. Optional: fill in Table names and columns, for example orders(id, customer_id, created_at, total).
3. Choose your database: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server, SQLite or BigQuery.
4. Run it, read the result, and copy it with one click.

The more exact your request, the closer the query gets to what you want. Say which table to read, which columns to return, how to filter the rows and how to sort them. A request like list the 10 newest orders from the last 30 days, with customer name and total gives the generator far more to work with than show orders.

If you want a step-by-step guide to plain English requests, see [SQL query generator from text](https://sql-generator.lazur.app/from-text).

sections.heading: Why the database choice matters
sections.body:
SQL is a shared language, but each database has its own details. A simple example is the row limit. SQL Server uses TOP, as in SELECT TOP 10 at the start of the query. PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite and BigQuery use LIMIT 10 at the end. A query written for one of these can fail on another.

**Choose the database you actually use.** If you are not sure, check the connection settings of the app or the tool where the query will run.

sections.heading: Check the query before you run it
sections.body:
Treat the output as a draft. Before you run it, check each table and column name against your real schema. Read the WHERE line to confirm the filter matches what you asked for. If there are JOIN lines, check that the keys they join on are the right columns.

Run the query on a copy of the database or on a small test table first. If the result is not what you expected, make the request more specific and generate again. Do not paste live personal or financial records into any tool to get help. Use made-up rows or only the column names, which is enough to get the shape of the query right.

Use the [text to SQL generator](https://sql-generator.lazur.app/from-text) in four steps.

You do not need to know SQL to write the request. You do need to know what you want back: which table, which columns, which rows to keep, and in what order. If you can say that in one or two sentences, you can get a usable query in one run. Keep the sentences plain. Words like recent or top are vague, so give a number of days or a number of rows instead.

sections.heading: Words that make a better request
sections.body:
A vague request gives a vague query. Compare these two.

- Weak: show sales.
- Better: total sales for each region over the last 30 days, highest total first, from the orders table.

Name the table, list the columns you want, state the date range in full, and say how many rows you need. Use the column names exactly as they appear in your database, because the generator builds the query from the names you give it. If a name is wrong, the query will use that wrong name too.

**The table and column box is the fastest fix.** It is optional, but a line such as orders(id, region, created_at, total) keeps the query close to your own setup.

sections.heading: When the SQL needs a second look
sections.body:
Read the result before you run it. Check that each table and column name exists in your database. Check that the WHERE line filters the rows you meant, for example the right date range or status. If you use GROUP BY, check that every column you return is either grouped or summarized.

Test the query on a copy of your data or on a small sample first. If the rows look wrong, change one part of your request at a time, such as the filter or the sort, and generate again. Changing one thing at a time shows you which change made the difference.

sections.heading: Pick the database first
sections.body:
The same request can produce different SQL for different databases. Row limits are one example. SQL Server writes SELECT TOP 10 at the start of the query, while PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite and BigQuery use LIMIT 10 at the end. Date functions and quoting rules also differ between databases.

**Choose the database before you generate.** That setting changes the syntax of the query, so a query for the wrong database can fail even when the logic is right.

sections.heading: What to check in the answer
sections.body:
Before you copy the SQL, look at the parts that usually go wrong. Check that the FROM line names the right table. Check that each column in the SELECT line exists and means what you think it means.
